questions.q: What has actually been proven and demonstrated about Shor's algorithm, as distinct from what remains unachieved?
options: The algorithm has never been run on any real quantum hardware, only simulated on classical computers
The algorithm's math is still unproven and under active dispute among researchers
The algorithm is mathematically sound and has been physically demonstrated factoring small numbers like 15 and 21 on real quantum hardware; what remains unachieved is running it at RSA-2048 scale
The algorithm has already been demonstrated breaking RSA-2048 in a research lab
questions.explain: Shor's algorithm is settled, published mathematics, verified in small-scale hardware demonstrations (factoring 15, 21) -- the gap to RSA-2048 is a scale-up problem, not a correctness problem.

questions.q: What is the widely cited Gidney & Ekerå (2019) estimate for breaking RSA-2048, and how should it be understood?
options: A number computed from scratch in this lesson using the N=15 toy example, scaled up linearly
An estimate of how many classical computers, not quantum computers, would be needed
Roughly 20 million noisy qubits running for about 8 hours, cited here as a specific literature estimate from a named 2019 paper, not a number computed in this lesson
An official international standards-body requirement for post-quantum migration deadlines
questions.explain: The 20-million-qubit, 8-hour figure comes from Gidney and Ekerå's published 2019 paper and is cited here explicitly as sourced literature, not derived independently.

questions.q: How do real quantum computers from the 2024-2026 era compare to the resource estimate needed to threaten RSA-2048?
options: Real hardware has qubit counts in the tens to low thousands range, several orders of magnitude short of the ~20 million qubits the estimate calls for, and those qubits are also noisy compared to what large-scale error-corrected computation requires
The qubit counts are roughly equal; only minor software optimization separates today's hardware from the estimate
Real hardware already exceeds the 20 million qubit estimate and is limited only by software
Real hardware has no qubits at all and remains purely theoretical
questions.explain: Current real devices fall several orders of magnitude short of the cited estimate's qubit count, and also lack the low error rates needed to sustain the deep circuits required.

questions.q: What does 'error-correction overhead' refer to, and why does it matter for this lesson's conclusion?
options: A term describing how long it takes to factor N=15 on a classical simulation
The cost in dollars of operating a quantum computer for one hour

The ratio of noisy physical qubits needed to build one reliable logical qubit, commonly cited in the hundreds to thousands -- it compounds with the raw qubit-count gap, making the hardware challenge even larger than qubit count alone suggests
The extra classical computing time needed to run continued fractions after measurement
questions.explain: Physical qubits are noisy; building one error-corrected logical qubit from them commonly requires hundreds to thousands of physical qubits, compounding with the already-large raw qubit-count gap.

questions.q: According to this lesson, where does the real blocker to breaking RSA-2048 with Shor's algorithm lie?
options: In the algorithm itself, which contains an unresolved mathematical flaw
In legal restrictions that prevent building large quantum computers
In the unavailability of the continued-fractions technique, which has not yet been invented
In hardware engineering -- insufficient qubit count and insufficiently low error rates -- not in any flaw or gap in the algorithm's mathematics
questions.explain: The lesson's central honesty point: the math (proven in Lessons 20-22) is not the obstacle. Qubit count and error rates -- engineering -- are the obstacle.
